## What you will be able to do

::: {.mm-outcomes-wrap}
- Write short, readable Python for scientific data: lists and dictionaries as lookup tables, functions with docstrings, f-strings for formatted output, `pathlib` for files, and tracebacks read from the bottom up.
- Store measurements in NumPy arrays, select them with slices and boolean masks, replace loops with vectorised arithmetic and broadcasting, and generate reproducible random numbers with a seeded generator.
- Recognise the $X$ (samples × features) / $y$ (targets) convention that every model in this course consumes.
- Load, inspect, filter, group, merge and reshape tables with pandas, and handle missing values and categorical columns deliberately rather than by accident.
- Draw histograms, scatter plots, box plots and small multiples with matplotlib and seaborn, with units on every axis and colours that work for everyone.
- Carry out an exploratory data analysis of the ESOL solubility dataset end to end, and repeat the workflow on the breast cancer Wisconsin dataset in the guided lab.
:::

## Check your understanding

The [ten-question checkpoint](checkpoint.html) checks shapes, indexing, data quality, plotting and the limits of exploratory analysis. Revisit any missed idea before starting Chapter 2.

## Before you start

::: {.prereq}
You need a working Python environment and the habit of running code in a notebook. If you have not done so, work through [Chapter 0](../ch00-start-here/index.html) and run the checks in [Setting up Python](../ch00-start-here/02-setup.html). The [self-check](../ch00-start-here/03-self-check.html) tests basic Python fluency. For copied episode cells, work from the repository root so `data/penguins.csv` resolves correctly.
:::

::: {.bridge audience="cs"}
If you already write Python for a living, skim [episode 1.1](01-python-refresher.html) for the scientific examples and the `pathlib` and f-string conventions this course uses, then start properly at [episode 1.2](02-numpy-arrays.html). NumPy's broadcasting rules and pandas' label-based indexing are where experienced programmers most often trip, so slow down there.
:::
